title: Engineering and Design Methodologies
purpose: Seed engineering/design methodology so Lantern can transform needs into requirements, constraints, architectures and prototypes; evaluate tradeoffs, verification, validation, safety, failure modes, maintainability and lifecycle; and iterate from evidence rather than treating implementation completion as success.

concepts.definition: A problem, goal or desired outcome expressed from a stakeholder/user/system perspective before committing to a specific solution.
A testable statement of required system behavior, property, interface or performance derived from needs and constraints.
A boundary limiting feasible solutions, such as compute, cost, time, safety, law, compatibility, ethics or physical limits.
A property to optimize or improve subject to requirements and constraints; multiple objectives can conflict.
High-level organization of components, responsibilities, interfaces and interactions chosen to satisfy requirements.
Declared boundary/contract through which components or users interact.
Purpose-built representation/implementation used to test assumptions, interactions, feasibility or user experience before full commitment.
Smallest implementation/test sufficient to resolve a high-value uncertainty; not necessarily a market product.
Evidence that an implementation satisfies specified requirements/design outputs: building the thing according to specification.
Evidence that the resulting system satisfies intended stakeholder needs/use context: building the right thing.
A design choice where improving one objective can worsen another; tradeoffs should expose objectives and weights rather than hide them.
Deliberate capacity/tolerance beyond nominal expected conditions to account for uncertainty/variation.
A specific way a component/system can fail to perform intended function or violate constraints.
Failure Modes and Effects Analysis: structured identification of potential failures, consequences, causes, detection and mitigation priorities.
Top-down analysis of combinations of failures/events that can produce an undesired outcome.
System property of retaining bounded useful/safe behavior when components/resources fail or degrade.
Design behavior intended to move toward a safer state when specified failures occur.
Iterative design grounded in users' goals, contexts, capabilities, accessibility and observed interaction rather than designer assumptions alone.
Observation/evaluation of representative users performing relevant tasks to identify interaction problems and validate design assumptions.
Ease/safety with which a system can be understood, diagnosed, repaired, modified and tested over its lifecycle.
Future cost/risk created by implementation/design shortcuts or accumulated complexity; debt may be intentional but should be visible.
Stages from concept/design through implementation, operation, maintenance, migration and retirement/decommissioning.
Links among stakeholder needs, requirements, design decisions, implementation components and verification/validation evidence.
Structured evaluation and recording of modifications, dependencies, risks, tests and rollback/migration requirements.

guards.reason: Requirements are interpretations/formalizations of needs and can be incomplete or wrong.
A system can meet its written specification while solving the wrong problem.
Usefulness does not prove all technical/safety/interface requirements.
Prototypes may omit reliability, security, scale, maintainability and edge conditions.
Improving one objective can regress other requirements/objectives.
Margins address specified uncertainty/ranges, not all failure modes.
Fail-safe mechanisms have assumptions/failure modes and reduce rather than erase risk.
Requests should be understood in context of underlying need, constraints, interactions and priorities.
Human-centered design tests assumptions with relevant users/context.
Debt can be an explicit bounded tradeoff when benefits, risks and repayment/containment are understood.
Additional features can increase complexity, resource use, failure surface and usability burden.
Migration, compatibility and incremental evolution should be evaluated before discarding working systems.
Engineering failure analysis examines interacting design, process, interface and environmental contributors before assigning cause.

invariants: Engineering begins with needs/problems and constraints, not preferred technologies.
Requirements should be testable and traceable to needs.
Verification and validation are distinct and both matter.
Design decisions preserve tradeoffs rather than hiding regressions behind one improved metric.
Prototypes are experiments for reducing uncertainty, not automatically production systems.
Safety is designed through layered controls, margins, failure analysis and graceful/fail-safe behavior rather than assumed from success cases.
Human-centered design tests designer assumptions against actual use/context.
Maintainability, migration and retirement are engineering concerns, not afterthoughts.
Technical debt is made visible with consequences and rationale.
Changes require dependency analysis, targeted tests and regression protection.
Working systems should evolve incrementally when that offers better risk/value than unnecessary rewrites.
Engineering evidence includes failures; failure is information for redesign rather than merely blame.

provenance.authoring_basis: Systems engineering, human-centered design, safety/reliability engineering, iterative/prototyping and lifecycle methodologies adapted to Lantern's incremental architecture and self-iteration goals.
